claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight HEA is a homogeneous, supersaturated, metastable solid solution with uniform elemental distribution and minimal intermetallic content.
Rapid solidification or mechanical alloying can produce the specified non-equilibrium initial state.
Thermal exposure causes the metastable solid solution to decompose by a diffusion-controlled transformation.
The diffusional transformation nucleates and grows intermetallic precipitates at grain boundaries and within grains.
Reported Mg-containing multi-principal-element alloys can contain intermetallic compounds.
Intermetallic precipitation sequesters passivating elements such as Al or Cr and depletes them from the surrounding continuous matrix.
Bulk elemental depletion can be associated with formation of a non-protective oxide in a high-entropy alloy.
Matrix depletion of Al or Cr impairs formation of a coherent protective Al2O3 or Cr2O3 scale.
A protective oxide-rich surface film can enhance passivation and reduce corrosion current density in an Mg-containing alloy.
Uniform elemental distribution in the initial state promotes formation of a continuous protective passivating oxide film.
The initial protective film gives the metastable state relatively low oxidation rates and enhanced corrosion resistance.
Annealing near 900 °C in air accelerates diffusion and intermetallic precipitation.
Relative to the initial state, the annealed alloy will contain visible intermetallic precipitates.
Relative to the initial state, annealing will reduce the continuity or alter the composition of the surface oxide scale.
Relative to the initial state, the annealed alloy will exhibit increased oxidation weight gain.
Relative to the initial state, the annealed alloy will exhibit higher corrosion current density in 3.5 wt.% NaCl.
The proposed mechanism operates when transformation kinetics become appreciable during extended thermal exposure around 900 °C.
An as-cast control and an annealed specimen from the same alloy can be compared using XRD, SEM-EDS, oxidation weight gain, and electrochemical polarization.
